body:
I will take a look at this in the next few days

I think the reasoning of this makes a lot of sense, and in the end the risk of it is essentially zero, the likelihood of actually running out of RID validators (or, with this change, causing them to loop around) is essentially none in any reasonable use of the engine (allocating an RID every millisecond it will take over 24 days, in order to run out in just 24 hours you have to allocate one every 40 us, which I can't really see in any non-destructive use)

The main reason I didn't just make this kind of change in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/74759 was that I didn't feel confident making the assessment of the risk and benefit of doing this, especially considering the extremely minimal relevance for all but cases that I'd consider non-reasonable use of the engine

The only concern I really can think of (and I'll take a look at the code tomorrow probably) is the practically infinitesimal risk of having a repeat RID, but the risk of that I'd consider negligible as well. This would be a case where you allocate an RID, store it away somewhere, free it, and then after the RIDs have looped around again you happen to run into the same one again, causing errors or confusion because it is no longer the "same" RID as it was before, but is also not invalid. But again the proportion of RIDs that are valid at any given time (in, once again, "reasonable" use, as opposed to destructive testing etc.) will be a tiny fraction of the total available values, so this is going to be essentially impossible

---

Tl;dr; Will look at this tomorrow, but I think any real risk or benefit is purely academic, and it'll be worth just "fixing" this problem properly for the extreme edge cases that might be affected by this, as regardless any risk caused by this change will affect essentially no users at essentially no time

> The main reason I didn't just make this kind of change in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/74759 was that I didn't feel confident making the assessment of the risk and benefit of doing this, especially considering the extremely minimal relevance for all but cases that I'd consider non-reasonable use of the engine

And that is totally fair lawnjelly, randomshaper, and me all reviewed the PR and felt the same way.

_Just a caveat first to say I'm not super familiar with the 4.x implementation of `RIDs` as I work mainly on 3.x, so the following is to the best of my current knowledge_.

After re-reading #74759 (I totally forgot reviewing it 2 years ago :blush: ), Pedro's comment https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/74759#issuecomment-1598496295 reminds me the problem here (sorry I'm a bit slow):

In conversation with @clayjohn I pointed out that with handles, as used more conventionally, you might store an ID and a revision (validator), say 24 bit for ID and 8 bit for revision.

Some reasons a `handle` is used over a pointer are:
* Data is relocatable (you can use e.g. a `Vector` to store the elements). The flip side of being relocatable like this is you must `get` the pointer each time to use it, and it assumes single thread access.

THIS DOESN'T TEND TO BE USED IN GODOT RIDS, as the objects are not assumed to be relocatable by client code. 

* You don't need to assign all the bits that you would with a pointer. Particularly with 64 bit pointers, are you going to need that many elements? Often you can use e.g. 24 bit.
* You can use extra bits to have some kind of "checksum" to detect invalid access. In most cases this will be a revision which increments each new allocation.

In most cases with handles the revision is used as a debug type _safety net_ to try and catch e.g. dangling handles. If you try and call `get` on a handle which has been freed, either the ID will be marked as unused, or if used, the revision will not match the data stored revision (as it will have been incremented on next allocation).

The important thing here is that **the revision is not usually considered reliable**. Due to rollover (say with 8 bit) you will get by chance some dangling handles that are not detected. The point is to detect most of these cases (particularly during development) and flag up errors. In theory in _release_ you could compile out the revisions and it would still work fine (but most don't do this as it is usually not the bottleneck, and the added safety is normally desired in release, say for libraries where the client code could make mistakes).

## Things that Godot 4 does differently

### Single validator counter
In conventional cases you store the revision in the handle _and on the data element itself_(or similar). This means that the revision is unique to the element being accessed, and rollover will only occur if that particular element (or owner in this case too) is being hammered.

In Godot 4 there is only a single validator that is stored globally. That makes it far more likely to overflow as every `RID` allocated increments the same counter.

Even a single validator _per owner_ would be better, but we probably can't currently as it is relying on this for the `is_owned` machinery. :thinking: 

### It RELIES on the validator
Conventional handles use handles for error detection but do not RELY on them. Because of the rollover behaviour there is a chance of collisions, and this is expected.

Godot 4 in particular is relying on the validator for ownership checks with `RID_Owners`. This means the penalty for validator collisions is potentially severe, and worse, these bugs will be hard to detect / pin down and may cause undefined behaviour.

In contrast, Godot 3 uses a different approach - each `RID` capable object must derive from `RID_Data`. This can tag extra data onto the object. We can actually tag a pointer to the owner onto the data element itself, which means we can look up whether an element is owned without relying on the validator.

## How typical handles SHOULD be used
Typical handles (at risk of revision collisions) should be treated as slightly safer pointers imo.
That means:
* They should be locally cleared after deleting the object (so there is no dangling handle)
* Deletion of objects should be propagated to all systems that might be holding a long term handle to that object, so that any dangling handles can also be cleared.

Generally this is why we advise using `ObjectID`s for longterm references to objects, as these are safe (in theory, haven't checked lol) to lookup and don't require propagating deletion notifications.

Currently I get the impression that the approach here in Godot is somewhat _wishy washy_, particularly as users themselves can create `RIDs` in script. Some contributors will be aware of the dangers of storing `RIDs` and collisions, and may be cleaning up on delete notifications from `free_RID` or similar. Some will not. Users will very likely not be aware.

## Some recommendations
In the light of this I would regard rollover behaviour here to some extent "playing with fire". It exchanges one type of problem (running out of validators, defined crash) for another (risk of collisions, undefined behaviour). It can be argued that the risk of collisions is super rare, but I'm not absolutely sure that's the case if there are some `RIDs` that are allocated early on and kept, and some `RIDs` with high churn.

_I think the highest risk of collisions will come from early allocated `RIDs` with low IDs and low validators, colliding with high churn `RIDs` from another owner that tends to keep the IDs low (maybe by deleting every frame, or something like that), and just after a rollover. But it's kind of hard to intuit the worst case scenario without some simulation or something. I suspect there are some situations where the probability is a lot higher than simplified math might predict, indeed you could set up a test case to do just this._

I suggested to clay checking behaviour by e.g. making the bit depth of the validator a `#define` and seeing what happens if we make this 8 bit instead of 32 bit. If it crashes it shows up potential problems. Another type of check would be starting the `validator` count close to rollover, or simply incrementing it by e.g. 65536 each time instead of 1.

I'm not quite sure yet the best way to proceed but wanted to summarise some of my thoughts this morning, (I'm _really not hugely familiar_ with the 4.x implementation of RIDs, so it's difficult for me to say more at this stage).

### Summary
I guess my current understanding is: Probably OK, but I wouldn't want to be in a plane flying with this software for auto-pilot. Would prefer longterm for the `RIDs` to be rewritten to engineer out this problem.

(You could also potentially temporarily at least cheat, and just make the `RIDs` 128 bit :smiling_imp: ).

BTW if we do go with this rollover, it could be worth putting in a `WARN_PRINT` when the rollover happens, just to make tracking down any related issues easier. I don't think anyone would object to this warning if it happened like super rarely.
